ego.name: Herman Hollerith
ego.summary: Herman Hollerith was a German-American statistician, inventor, and businessman who developed electromechanical punched-card tabulating machines. His system accelerated the 1890 United States census. The Tabulating Machine Company later entered the company renamed International Business Machines in 1924.

connections.relationship_description: Hollerith's father was a German immigrant, schoolteacher, and Lutheran minister who raised him in Buffalo, New York.
connections.notes: Georg Hollerith had participated in the German revolutions of 1848–1849.

connections.relationship_description: Franciska Brunn Hollerith was Hollerith's German immigrant mother and part of the Buffalo household in which he spent his early childhood.
Billings suggested using electrical connections to operate counters during Census Office work. Hollerith developed the suggestion into his punched-card tabulating system.
connections.notes: Billings supplied the originating suggestion. Hollerith designed and patented the practical electromechanical system.

connections.relationship_description: Flint arranged the 1911 merger that placed the Tabulating Machine Company in Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company. Hollerith received $1.2 million in the transaction.
connections.notes: Hollerith remained associated with the successor company as a consulting engineer until 1921.

connections.relationship_description: Porter was Superintendent of the Census from 1889 to 1893 and oversaw the 1890 census, whose compilation used Hollerith's tabulating machines.
Wright succeeded Robert P. Porter as Superintendent of the Census in 1893. He oversaw continuing work on the 1890 census tabulation that used Hollerith’s system.
Wines was among the officials overseeing the statistical work of the 1900 United States census, for which Hollerith's company again supplied tabulating equipment.
Willcox shared oversight of the 1900 United States census statistics, connecting him professionally with the census work supported by Hollerith's tabulators.
As president of Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company from 1914, Watson led the successor business while Hollerith served as a consulting engineer until his 1921 retirement.
connections.notes: Watson later renamed the company International Business Machines in 1924.

connections.relationship_description: Fairchild chaired Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company during part of Hollerith's tenure as its consulting engineer after the 1911 amalgamation.
connections.notes: Fairchild ran CTR from 1911 until 1912 and remained its chairman during the early Watson era.

connections.relationship_description: Heidinger founded Deutsche Hollerith-Maschinen Gesellschaft in Berlin in 1910 as a licensee of Hollerith's Tabulating Machine Company, distributing and leasing Hollerith punched-card equipment in Germany.
connections.notes: The relationship extended Hollerith's technology into the German market before the later incorporation of the business into IBM's corporate structure.

category_summaries.summary: Hollerith grew up in Buffalo in a household formed by German immigrants. His father combined school teaching with Lutheran ministry. The family background preceded Hollerith’s entry into New York’s technical education system at about fifteen.

Census Office work gave Hollerith a practical problem in handling large collections of statistics. John Shaw Billings suggested electrical counting. Hollerith turned that suggestion into a punched-card system and secured patents for its operation.

Federal census work put Hollerith’s machines to use on national population statistics. The 1890 census used his equipment under Robert P. Porter’s administration. Later census officials connected the company’s machines with the continuing work of the 1890 census and the 1900 census.

The Tabulating Machine Company leased machines and sold cards to census bureaus, insurance companies, and other customers. Charles Ranlett Flint placed the company in Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company in 1911. Hollerith remained a consulting engineer until 1921 while the successor company grew under new leadership.
